claim: MDCK cells stably expressing Lifeact-GFP exhibited a typical apical actin organization with clustered microvilli prior to shear stress.
source: Prior to shear stress, MDCK cells stably expressing Lifeact-GFP exhibited a typical apical actin organization with clustered microvilli (Klingner et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation about MDCK cells before shear stress, with citation to prior work.

claim: Exposure to fluid flow of 10–20 dyn/cm2 induced the formation of a highly transient perinuclear actin ring in MDCK cells.
source: Immediately upon exposure to fluid flow of 10–20 dyn/cm2 we observed the formation of a highly transient perinuclear actin ring, which only remained for a few minutes (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: Direct observation reported in text and shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: A similar phenomenon of perinuclear actin ring formation was recently reported in fibroblasts.
source: A similar phenomenon was recently reported in fibroblasts (Shao et al., 2015), but its consequences for cell organization were not further explored.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study that reported similar observations.

claim: Actin reorganization in MDCK cells upon shear stress was preceded by a strong intracellular Ca2+ pulse.
source: Upon induction of shear stress, actin reorganization was preceded by a strong intracellular Ca2+ pulse (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Direct measurement shown in Figure 1A,B with calcium indicator Fluo-4.

claim: Exposure to 0.3 µM ionomycin induced the formation of perinuclear actin rings and reduction of cortical actin within 60 s in MDCK cells.
source: Indeed, exposure to as little as 0.3 µM ionomycin induced the formation of perinuclear actin rings and reduction of cortical actin within 60 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with ionomycin treatment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a virtually simultaneous decrease of actin filaments at the apical cortex during perinuclear actin ring formation.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to the previous report, we found a virtually simultaneous decrease of actin filaments at the apical cortex (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct observation reported in text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Actin rapidly reverted to its cortical distribution within 60 s following the initial reorganization.
source: As for the transient shear stress response, actin rapidly reverted to its cortical distribution within the following 60 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct observation of time course shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rapid relocation of actin from the cell cortex to the nuclear periphery occurred within 60 s in all tested mammalian cell lines upon ionomycin treatment.
source: In all instances, rapid relocation of actin from the cell cortex to the nuclear periphery occurred within 60 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Video 2).
evidence: Observation across multiple cell types shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Video 2.

claim: Human MCF-7 breast cancer cells exhibited the strongest CaAR response.
source: We observed the strongest response for human MCF-7 breast cancer cells (Figure 1D, Video 3) and therefore decided to focus on this cell line for further studies.
evidence: Comparative observation across cell lines shown in Figure 1D and Video 3.

claim: Actin reorganization in MCF-7 cells was not influenced by Lifeact-GFP expression.
source: Actin reorganization in MCF-7 cells was not influenced by Lifeact-GFP expression, as we observed an identical response in non-transfected cells stained with Alexa Fluor 647-phalloidin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Control experiment comparing transfected and non-transfected cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon calcium influx, actin filaments formed not only at the nuclear periphery, but throughout the cell.
source: Importantly, we found that, upon calcium influx, actin filaments formed not only at the nuclear periphery, but throughout the cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and all along the endoplasmic reticulum (ER, Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1E.

claim: Actin filaments formed all along the endoplasmic reticulum upon calcium influx.
source: Importantly, we found that, upon calcium influx, actin filaments formed not only at the nuclear periphery, but throughout the cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and all along the endoplasmic reticulum (ER, Figure 1E).
evidence: Direct observation with ER marker shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Activation of calcium influx using ATP efficiently induced actin rearrangement.
source: As expected, activation of calcium influx using physiological ligands for G-protein-coupled receptors, such as ATP or bradykinin efficiently induced actin rearrangement (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with ATP treatment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Activation of calcium influx using bradykinin efficiently induced actin rearrangement.
source: As expected, activation of calcium influx using physiological ligands for G-protein-coupled receptors, such as ATP or bradykinin efficiently induced actin rearrangement (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with bradykinin treatment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In most cells release of calcium from ER stores activates store-operated calcium entry from the extracellular environment.
source: In most cells release of calcium from ER stores activates store-operated calcium entry from the extracellular environment (Hogan and Rao, 2015).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citation.

claim: Blocking uptake of Ca2+ into the ER with thapsigargin in the presence of high extracellular Ca2+ induced actin rearrangement.
source: Hence, blocking uptake of Ca2+ into the ER with thapsigargin - in the presence of high extracellular Ca2+ - also induced actin rearrangement (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with thapsigargin treatment shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Perforation of the plasma membrane by localized mechanical disruption (atomic force microscopy, AFM) efficiently induced cortex to ER actin reorganization.
source: Finally, perforation of the plasma membrane by localized mechanical disruption (atomic force microscopy, AFM) or laser-induced ablation efficiently induced cortex to ER actin reorganization (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with AFM shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Perforation of the plasma membrane by laser-induced ablation efficiently induced cortex to ER actin reorganization.
source: Finally, perforation of the plasma membrane by localized mechanical disruption (atomic force microscopy, AFM) or laser-induced ablation efficiently induced cortex to ER actin reorganization (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with laser ablation shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CaAR is initiated within seconds after Ca2+ influx in all tested cell types.
source: In all cell types that we tested, CaAR was initiated within seconds after Ca2+ influx (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and not shown).
evidence: Direct observation across multiple cell types shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Actin concentration at the ER reached its maximum within less than 1 min during CaAR.
source: Actin concentration at the ER reached its maximum within less than 1 min and reverted back to the original state within less than 5 min.
evidence: Direct measurement of kinetics reported in text.

claim: Actin concentration at the ER reverted back to the original state within less than 5 min during CaAR.
source: Actin concentration at the ER reached its maximum within less than 1 min and reverted back to the original state within less than 5 min.
evidence: Direct measurement of kinetics reported in text.

claim: Actin recruitment to the ER followed a typical three-phase kinetics characterized by a rapid increase, a plateau and a slower decrease.
source: Actin recruitment to the ER followed a typical three-phase kinetics characterized by a rapid increase, a plateau and a slower decrease (Figure 2A).
evidence: Direct observation of kinetics shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The actin increase at the ER was significantly faster for cells grown in serum compared to serum-starved cells.
source: The actin increase at the ER was significantly faster for cells grown in serum or at 37°C.
evidence: Comparative measurement under different conditions reported in text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The actin increase at the ER was significantly faster at 37°C compared to room temperature.
source: The actin increase at the ER was significantly faster for cells grown in serum or at 37°C.
evidence: Comparative measurement under different conditions reported in text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stimulation of MCF-7 and HeLa cells with 50 µM ATP led to faster increase than for ionomycin.
source: Also, the stimulation of MCF-7 and HeLa cells with 50 µM ATP led to faster increase than for ionomycin (Figure 2B, Table 1).
evidence: Comparative measurement shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Addition of serum or ATP had little effect on the rate of decrease or the amplitude of the CaAR reaction.
source: In contrast, addition of serum or ATP had little effect on the rate of decrease or the amplitude of the reaction (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparative measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CaAR plateau was shortened at 37°C compared to room temperature.
source: Finally, the CaAR plateau was shortened at 37°C, for cells grown in serum and upon stimulation with ATP (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparative measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CaAR plateau was shortened for cells grown in serum compared to serum-starved cells.
source: Finally, the CaAR plateau was shortened at 37°C, for cells grown in serum and upon stimulation with ATP (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparative measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CaAR plateau was shortened upon stimulation with ATP compared to ionomycin.
source: Finally, the CaAR plateau was shortened at 37°C, for cells grown in serum and upon stimulation with ATP (Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparative measurement shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment of HeLa cells with ionomycin induced very strong and long-lasting CaAR response.
source: Treatment of HeLa cells with ionomycin induced very strong and long-lasting CaAR response (Figure 2B), indicating that these cells could not as efficiently remove Ca2+ from the cytosol.
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2B with interpretation.

claim: All kinetic parameters of CaAR remained within a three-fold range despite specific differences between conditions.
source: Most importantly, despite the specific differences described above, all kinetic parameters of CaAR remained within a three-fold range (Figure 2B), highlighting the robust and stereotypic nature of the response.
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ levels in MCF-7 cells increased 3.59 ± 0.84 fold upon exposure to ionomycin.
source: We found that cytosolic Ca2+ levels in MCF-7 cells increased 2- to 4-fold upon exposure to ionomycin (3.59 ± 0.84 fold, n = 31) or ATP (2.82 ± 0.67 fold, n = 54), which induced CaAR in virtually all cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct measurement with Fura-2 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ levels in MCF-7 cells increased 2.82 ± 0.67 fold upon exposure to ATP.
source: We found that cytosolic Ca2+ levels in MCF-7 cells increased 2- to 4-fold upon exposure to ionomycin (3.59 ± 0.84 fold, n = 31) or ATP (2.82 ± 0.67 fold, n = 54), which induced CaAR in virtually all cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct measurement with Fura-2 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ionomycin and ATP induced CaAR in virtually all MCF-7 cells.
source: We found that cytosolic Ca2+ levels in MCF-7 cells increased 2- to 4-fold upon exposure to ionomycin (3.59 ± 0.84 fold, n = 31) or ATP (2.82 ± 0.67 fold, n = 54), which induced CaAR in virtually all cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Induction of CaAR was completely prevented in Ca2+-free medium.
source: Induction of CaAR was completely prevented in Ca2+-free medium, but could be restored within 1 min by addition of Ca2+ (not shown).
evidence: Direct experimental observation reported in text.

claim: CaAR could be restored within 1 min by addition of Ca2+ to Ca2+-free medium.
source: Induction of CaAR was completely prevented in Ca2+-free medium, but could be restored within 1 min by addition of Ca2+ (not shown).
evidence: Direct experimental observation reported in text.

claim: Release of calcium from ER stores with thapsigargin in Ca2+-free medium led to a modest cytosolic Ca2+ increase of 1.26 ± 0.08 fold.
source: In Ca2+-free medium, release of calcium from ER stores with thapsigargin could not be enhanced by store-operated calcium entry and led to a modest cytosolic Ca2+ increase of 1.26 ± 0.08 fold (n = 31).
evidence: Direct measurement with Fura-2 reported in text.

claim: A cytosolic Ca2+ increase of 1.26 ± 0.08 fold was insufficient to induce CaAR.
source: In Ca2+-free medium, release of calcium from ER stores with thapsigargin could not be enhanced by store-operated calcium entry and led to a modest cytosolic Ca2+ increase of 1.26 ± 0.08 fold (n = 31). This was insufficient to induce CaAR (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CaAR induction requires a threshold level of intracellular Ca2+ that can only be reached by influx from the extracellular environment.
source: These results indicate that CaAR induction requires a threshold level of intracellular Ca2+ that can only be reached by influx from the extracellular environment.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with Ca2+-free medium and thapsigargin.

claim: The subcortical regions (800 nm below the plasma membrane) of MCF-7 cells treated with ionomycin became markedly stiffer during CaAR.
source: Despite the observed transient reduction of cortical actin, we found that the subcortical regions (800 nm below the plasma membrane) of MCF-7 cells treated with ionomycin became markedly stiffer during CaAR, mirroring greater levels of actin recruitment at the ER (Figure 2D).
evidence: Direct measurement by AFM shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Random as well as directed motion of lysosomes was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset.
source: Random as well as directed motion of lysosomes (Figure 2E), mitochondria and the ER network (Figure 2F) was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset and resumed after actin returned to the cell cortex (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Random as well as directed motion of mitochondria was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset.
source: Random as well as directed motion of lysosomes (Figure 2E), mitochondria and the ER network (Figure 2F) was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset and resumed after actin returned to the cell cortex (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Random as well as directed motion of the ER network was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset.
source: Random as well as directed motion of lysosomes (Figure 2E), mitochondria and the ER network (Figure 2F) was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset and resumed after actin returned to the cell cortex (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Organelle motion resumed after actin returned to the cell cortex following CaAR.
source: Random as well as directed motion of lysosomes (Figure 2E), mitochondria and the ER network (Figure 2F) was abolished within a few seconds of CaAR onset and resumed after actin returned to the cell cortex (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Lysosomes were trapped within a cytosol-filling actin mesh that corresponded to the transient ER-based actin filaments during CaAR.
source: When simultaneously observing CaAR and lysosome motility we found the organelles trapped within a cytosol-filling actin mesh that corresponded to the transient ER-based actin filaments (Video 4).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Video 4.

claim: Lysosomes were immobilized in cells treated with 50 µM blebbistatin.
source: Lysosomes were also immobilized in cells treated with 50 µM blebbistatin arguing against a prominent role of actomyosin contractility for organelle freezing (Figure 2G).
evidence: Direct observation with blebbistatin treatment shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Actomyosin contractility does not play a prominent role in organelle freezing during CaAR.
source: Lysosomes were also immobilized in cells treated with 50 µM blebbistatin arguing against a prominent role of actomyosin contractility for organelle freezing (Figure 2G).
evidence: Inference from blebbistatin experiment shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Forces above 50 nN were able to robustly induce CaAR multiple times in a single cell using pointy AFM tips.
source: Forces above 50 nN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) were able to robustly induce CaAR multiple times in a single cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 5) with a refractory period of 30–60 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the time scale of actin recruitment at the ER.
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D and Video 5.

claim: CaAR has a refractory period of 30–60 s when induced multiple times in a single cell.
source: Forces above 50 nN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) were able to robustly induce CaAR multiple times in a single cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 5) with a refractory period of 30–60 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the time scale of actin recruitment at the ER.
evidence: Direct measurement shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells directly adjacent to AFM-manipulated cells also exhibited CaAR.
source: When using localized CaAR stimulation by AFM we frequently observed that cells directly adjacent to the manipulated cells also reacted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Nearly all cells within 60–150 µm of the ablation site exhibited CaAR in MCF-7 monolayers.
source: Strikingly, we found that nearly all cells within 60–150 µm of the ablation site exhibited CaAR (Figure 2H).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CaAR was observed in cells that were not in direct contact with the ablated cell.
source: This was also observed for cells that were not in direct contact with the ablated cell (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, Video 6).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Video 6.

claim: Ca2+ signals can be propagated across tissue sections and cell layers via ATP.
source: Previous reports have shown that Ca2+ signals can be propagated across tissue sections and cell layers via ATP (Frame and de Feijter, 1997; Schwiebert, 2000).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citations.

claim: Distant cells were no longer able to respond to cell ablation after the medium had been saturated with 100 µM ATP.
source: Indeed, distant cells were no longer able to respond to cell ablation after the medium had been saturated with 100 µM ATP (Figure 2I), indicating that ATP release and associated Ca2+ influx is responsible for the propagation of CaAR.
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ATP release and associated Ca2+ influx is responsible for the propagation of CaAR.
source: Indeed, distant cells were no longer able to respond to cell ablation after the medium had been saturated with 100 µM ATP (Figure 2I), indicating that ATP release and associated Ca2+ influx is responsible for the propagation of CaAR.
evidence: Inference from ATP saturation experiment shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Both G-actin sequestration by latrunculin A and actin filament disruption by cytochalasin D completely blocked CaAR.
source: Accordingly, both G-actin sequestration by latrunculin A (LatA) and actin filament disruption by cytochalasin D (CytoD) completely blocked CaAR (Figure 3A, Video 7).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3A and Video 7.

claim: Inverted formin 2 (INF2) is the only actin nucleator that has been shown to be localized at the ER.
source: The only actin nucleator that has been shown to be localized at the ER is inverted formin 2 (INF2) (Chhabra and Higgs, 2006), and this nucleator has also been shown to mediate the formation of perinuclear actin filaments in 3T3 fibroblasts (Shao et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citations.

claim: INF2 has been shown to mediate the formation of perinuclear actin filaments in 3T3 fibroblasts.
source: The only actin nucleator that has been shown to be localized at the ER is inverted formin 2 (INF2) (Chhabra and Higgs, 2006), and this nucleator has also been shown to mediate the formation of perinuclear actin filaments in 3T3 fibroblasts (Shao et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citation.

claim: INF2 was localized to the ER in MCF-7 and HeLa cells.
source: Indeed, in MCF-7 and HeLa cells, INF2 was localized to the ER, as shown either by immunofluorescence (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or when expressing the full-length INF2-CAAX isoform fused to GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct observation by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: A constitutively active point mutant of INF2 (A149D) induced strong actin staining at the ER.
source: A constitutively active point mutant of INF2 (A149D, (Korobova et al., 2013) induced the previously shown strong actin staining at the ER (Ramabhadran et al., 2013), which was not further increased by the addition of ionomycin (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct observation with mutant INF2 shown in Figure 3C, with citations to prior work.

claim: Actin staining at the ER induced by constitutively active INF2 (A149D) was not further increased by the addition of ionomycin.
source: A constitutively active point mutant of INF2 (A149D, (Korobova et al., 2013) induced the previously shown strong actin staining at the ER (Ramabhadran et al., 2013), which was not further increased by the addition of ionomycin (Figure 3C).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CaAR was completely blocked in HeLa cells that were depleted for INF2.
source: Strikingly, CaAR was completely blocked in HeLa cells that were depleted for INF2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Direct observation in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: INF2 knock-down blocked actin decrease at the cell cortex during CaAR.
source: Notably, INF2 knock-down also blocked actin decrease at the cell cortex (Figure 3E), increase in cell stiffness detected by AFM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and freezing of organelle motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: Direct observation in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: INF2 knock-down blocked increase in cell stiffness detected by AFM during CaAR.
source: Notably, INF2 knock-down also blocked actin decrease at the cell cortex (Figure 3E), increase in cell stiffness detected by AFM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and freezing of organelle motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: Direct measurement by AFM in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: INF2 knock-down blocked freezing of organelle motility during CaAR.
source: Notably, INF2 knock-down also blocked actin decrease at the cell cortex (Figure 3E), increase in cell stiffness detected by AFM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and freezing of organelle motility (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: Direct observation in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Both the CAAX- and nonCAAX human isoforms of INF2 were able to rescue the INF2 knockout and support efficient CaAR reactions.
source: Interestingly, both isoforms were able to rescue the knock out and to support efficient CaAR reactions (Figure 3F), indicating that ER-localization was not essential for actin reorganization.
evidence: Direct observation in rescue experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ER-localization of INF2 was not essential for actin reorganization during CaAR.
source: Interestingly, both isoforms were able to rescue the knock out and to support efficient CaAR reactions (Figure 3F), indicating that ER-localization was not essential for actin reorganization.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments with both INF2 isoforms shown in Figure 3F.

claim: GFP-INF2-CAAX expressed in HEK293 cells specifically interacts with immobilised calmodulin.
source: Co-precipitation analyses showed that GFP-INF2 expressed in HEK293 cells indeed specifically bound to immobilized calmodulin, and that this interaction was Ca2+-dependent (Figure 3G).
evidence: Direct biochemical experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The interaction between GFP-INF2 and calmodulin was Ca2+-dependent.
source: Co-precipitation analyses showed that GFP-INF2 expressed in HEK293 cells indeed specifically bound to immobilized calmodulin, and that this interaction was Ca2+-dependent (Figure 3G).
evidence: Direct biochemical experiment shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with blebbistatin did not inhibit or slow down CaAR.
source: However, pretreatment of cells with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin or with the microtubule disrupting drug nocodazole did not inhibit or slow down CaAR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with nocodazole did not inhibit or slow down CaAR.
source: However, pretreatment of cells with the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin or with the microtubule disrupting drug nocodazole did not inhibit or slow down CaAR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CaAR is largely dependent on the calcium-regulated actin nucleator INF2.
source: In summary, our results indicate that CaAR is largely dependent on a single factor – the calcium-regulated actin nucleator INF2.
evidence: Summary conclusion from INF2 knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: INF2 is not only an actin nucleator and elongator, but also a very potent severing and actin-depolymerizing factor.
source: Interestingly, the key regulator of CaAR, INF2, is a unique molecule that can at the same time stimulate actin nucleation, elongation, severing and depolymerization (Gurel et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citation.

claim: CaAR does not lead to the equal reduction of all cortical actin structures.
source: It is important to note that CaAR does not lead to the equal reduction of all cortical actin structures. Stable actin assemblies such as stress fibers were much less affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Video 8).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 8.

claim: Stable actin assemblies such as stress fibers were much less affected by CaAR than other cortical actin structures.
source: It is important to note that CaAR does not lead to the equal reduction of all cortical actin structures. Stable actin assemblies such as stress fibers were much less affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Video 8).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Video 8.

claim: There was no apparent delay between ER and cell cortex reactions during CaAR.
source: Also, despite their opposite slopes, there was no apparent delay between ER and cell cortex reactions and they followed the calcium signal with the same offset (Figure 4A).
evidence: Direct observation from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ER and cell cortex reactions followed the calcium signal with the same offset during CaAR.
source: Also, despite their opposite slopes, there was no apparent delay between ER and cell cortex reactions and they followed the calcium signal with the same offset (Figure 4A).
evidence: Direct observation from kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The duration of Ca2+ influx was directly correlated with the kinetics of actin reorganization at both ER and cell cortex.
source: In addition, the duration of Ca2+ influx was directly correlated with the kinetics of actin reorganization at both locations (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct observation from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The actin filament assembly and disassembly at the ER and cell cortex are tightly coupled during CaAR.
source: These observations indicate that the actin filament assembly and disassembly at the ER and cell cortex are tightly coupled.
evidence: Inference from kinetic observations.

claim: The t1/2 for recovery of actin-GFP at the cortex of MCF-7 cells was 14.48 ± 7.21 s.
source: The experimentally measured t1/2 for recovery of actin-GFP at the cortex of MCF-7 cells was quite fast, at 14.48 ± 7.21 s (n = 79).
evidence: Direct measurement by FRAP reported in text.

claim: The stochastic model predicted that including Ca2+- or INF2-dependent actin depolymerization strongly increased the amplitude and speed of actin reorganization at both cortex and ER.
source: Interestingly, the model predicted that including Ca2+- or INF2-dependent actin depolymerization into the model strongly increased the amplitude and speed of actin reorganization at both cortex and ER (solid curves in Figure 4D).
evidence: Prediction from computational model shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CaAR kinetics were strongly reduced in cells expressing the INF2 WH2-mutant (3L: L976A, L977A, L986A) with reduced depolymerization activity.
source: Strikingly CaAR kinetics were strongly reduced in cells expressing the 3L mutant. The resulting changes were comparable to the situation without Ca2+-mediated depolymerization predicted by the model (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Direct experimental observation with mutant INF2 shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The amplitude and the speed of reorganization were strongly reduced for both ER and cell cortex in cells expressing the INF2 3L mutant.
source: The amplitude and the speed of reorganization were strongly reduced for both, ER and cell cortex (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: The observed kinetics of CaAR can be quantitatively explained by a competition scenario with constitutively active cortical actin nucleators and Ca2+-activated INF2 at the ER.
source: In summary, our simulations indicate that the observed kinetics of CaAR can be quantitatively explained by a competition scenario with constitutively active cortical actin nucleators and Ca2+-activated INF2 at the ER.
evidence: Conclusion from computational modeling and experimental validation.

claim: The depolymerization activity of INF2 provides additional optimization for CaAR kinetics.
source: Importantly, the depolymerization activity of INF2 provides additional optimization for CaAR kinetics.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling and mutant experiments.

claim: Fractionation of MCF-7 cell extracts revealed a modest increase in the global F/G-actin ratio during CaAR.
source: Indeed, fractionation of MCF-7 cell extracts revealed a modest increase in the global F/G-actin ratio during CaAR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Direct biochemical measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The levels of actin at the cortex of MCF-7 cells were increased after completion of CaAR relative to those at the outset of CaAR.
source: In addition, the levels of actin at the cortex of MCF-7 cells were increased after completion of CaAR relative to those at the outset of CaAR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Within a minute of Ca2+ influx and CaAR onset, MRTF-A translocated into the nucleus in >95% of MCF-7 cells.
source: Indeed, we found that within a minute of Ca2+ influx and CaAR onset, MRTF-A translocated into the nucleus in >95% of MCF-7 cells, and remained there for up to 30 min (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Direct observation by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: MRTF-A remained in the nucleus for up to 30 min after translocation during CaAR.
source: Indeed, we found that within a minute of Ca2+ influx and CaAR onset, MRTF-A translocated into the nucleus in >95% of MCF-7 cells, and remained there for up to 30 min (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Direct observation by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: MRTF-A translocation occurred in HeLa cells during CaAR.
source: MRTF-A translocation also occurred in HeLa cells and was blocked upon INF2 knock-down (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MRTF-A translocation was blocked upon INF2 knock-down in HeLa cells.
source: MRTF-A translocation also occurred in HeLa cells and was blocked upon INF2 knock-down (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct observation in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MRTF-A translocation was inhibited when CaAR was blocked by treatment with LatA.
source: When we blocked CaAR by treatment with LatA, MRTF-A translocation was also inhibited (Figure 5D).
evidence: Direct observation with LatA treatment shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment with CytoD induced CaAR-independent translocation of MRTF-A.
source: In contrast, treatment with CytoD induced CaAR-independent translocation of MRTF-A (Figure 5E), consistent with previous reports (Descot et al., 2009).
evidence: Direct observation with CytoD treatment shown in Figure 5E, with citation to prior work.

claim: RNA levels of CTGF were strongly increased upon CaAR induction by ionomycin, reaching a maximum at 1 hr.
source: RNA levels of two known SRF targets, CTGF and NR4R3, were strongly increased upon CaAR induction by ionomycin, reaching a maximum at 1 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct measurement by RT-PCR shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RNA levels of NR4R3 were strongly increased upon CaAR induction by ionomycin, reaching a maximum at 1 hr.
source: RNA levels of two known SRF targets, CTGF and NR4R3, were strongly increased upon CaAR induction by ionomycin, reaching a maximum at 1 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct measurement by RT-PCR shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A 10 min pulse of ionomycin was sufficient to decrease the expression of 478 genes by more than 1.5 fold.
source: We found that a 10 min pulse of ionomycin was sufficient to decrease the expression of 478 genes and enhance the expression of 405 genes by more than 1.5 fold (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Direct measurement by transcriptome analysis.

claim: A 10 min pulse of ionomycin was sufficient to enhance the expression of 405 genes by more than 1.5 fold.
source: We found that a 10 min pulse of ionomycin was sufficient to decrease the expression of 478 genes and enhance the expression of 405 genes by more than 1.5 fold (Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Direct measurement by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Treatment with LatA on its own had very little effect on gene expression.
source: Treatment with LatA on its own had very little effect, but upregulation of 88 ionomycin-induced genes was strongly inhibited by LatA (Figure 5—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Direct measurement by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Upregulation of 88 ionomycin-induced genes was strongly inhibited by LatA.
source: Treatment with LatA on its own had very little effect, but upregulation of 88 ionomycin-induced genes was strongly inhibited by LatA (Figure 5—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: Direct measurement by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Nearly half of the CaAR-regulated genes that were inhibited by LatA are known SRF targets.
source: Nearly half of these genes are known SRF targets and about one third were also induced by the SRF activator CytoD (Figure 5G).
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: About one third of the CaAR-regulated genes that were inhibited by LatA were also induced by the SRF activator CytoD.
source: Nearly half of these genes are known SRF targets and about one third were also induced by the SRF activator CytoD (Figure 5G).
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Many of the CaAR-regulated genes were associated with genes involved in cytoskeletal organization, calcium regulation, cell signaling and regulation of cell adhesion.
source: In agreement with the reported functions of SRF, many of the identified transcriptional changes were associated with genes involved in cytoskeletal organization, calcium regulation, cell signaling and regulation of cell adhesion (Figure 5G).
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: More than 60% of the CaAR-regulated genes have been associated with cancer.
source: More than 60% of the CaAR-regulated genes have been associated with cancer and more than one-third have been implicated in cellular stress responses, cell differentiation, cell migration or inflammation (Figure 5G).
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: More than one-third of the CaAR-regulated genes have been implicated in cellular stress responses, cell differentiation, cell migration or inflammation.
source: More than 60% of the CaAR-regulated genes have been associated with cancer and more than one-third have been implicated in cellular stress responses, cell differentiation, cell migration or inflammation (Figure 5G).
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: SRF is known to respond to actin changes mediated through Rho GTPases.
source: SRF is known to respond to actin changes mediated through Rho GTPases (Treisman et al., 1998).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citation.

claim: CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the ROCK inhibitor Y27632.
source: However, we found that CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the ROCK inhibitor Y27632, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) or by the CaM kinase inhibitors KN62 and KN93 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA).
source: However, we found that CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the ROCK inhibitor Y27632, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) or by the CaM kinase inhibitors KN62 and KN93 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the CaM kinase inhibitors KN62 and KN93.
source: However, we found that CaAR-mediated induction of CTGF was not affected by the ROCK inhibitor Y27632, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporin A (CsA) or by the CaM kinase inhibitors KN62 and KN93 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Addition of serum did not induce CaAR in MCF-7 cells.
source: Importantly, all CaAR transcriptome experiments were performed in serum-starved cells and addition of serum did not induce CaAR in MCF-7 cells.
evidence: Direct experimental observation reported in text.

claim: Treatment of cells with Y27632 did not affect CaAR.
source: In addition, treatment of cells with Y27632, the Rho1 inhibitor C3 transferase or with CsA did not affect CaAR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Treatment of cells with the Rho1 inhibitor C3 transferase did not affect CaAR.
source: In addition, treatment of cells with Y27632, the Rho1 inhibitor C3 transferase or with CsA did not affect CaAR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Treatment of cells with CsA did not affect CaAR.
source: In addition, treatment of cells with Y27632, the Rho1 inhibitor C3 transferase or with CsA did not affect CaAR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Direct experimental observation shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CaAR mediates SRF activation through actin reorganization via a Ca2+-dependent pathway distinct from the previously described SRF activation involving Rho, ROCK and mDia.
source: Our results therefore indicate that CaAR mediates SRF activation through actin reorganization, but via a Ca2+-dependent pathway distinct from the previously described SRF activation involving Rho, ROCK and mDia (Baarlink et al., 2013; Copeland and Treisman, 2002).
evidence: Conclusion from inhibitor experiments with citations to prior work.

claim: Laser ablation of HeLa cells led to accumulation of actin at the site of membrane damage in more than 90% of the cases.
source: When we examined the cellular consequences of CaAR in laser ablation experiments with HeLa cells, we observed accumulation of actin at the site of membrane damage in more than 90% of the cases (Figure 6A, Video 9).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6A and Video 9.

claim: Actin accumulation at the site of membrane damage typically occurred after completion of CaAR.
source: This accumulation was reminiscent of previously observed wound repair processes (Clark et al., 2009; McNeil, 2002) and typically occurred after completion of CaAR (Figure 6B).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6B, with citations to prior work.

claim: Upon knock-down of INF2, HeLa cells did not undergo CaAR and were completely unable to recruit actin to the site of membrane wounding.
source: Upon knock-down of INF2, HeLa cells did not undergo CaAR and were also completely unable to recruit actin to the site of membrane wounding (Figure 6C).
evidence: Direct observation in INF2 knockdown cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Membrane damage was repaired within a few seconds of damage induction.
source: Importantly, membrane damage as measured by uptake of propidium iodide or FM4-64 was repaired within a few seconds of damage induction (not shown).
evidence: Direct experimental observation reported in text.

claim: Actin accumulation at wound sites was not required for membrane sealing but for a later step in wound repair, possibly cortex reassembly.
source: Actin accumulation was therefore not required for membrane sealing but for a later step in wound repair, possibly cortex reassembly.
evidence: Inference from timing of membrane sealing vs actin accumulation.

claim: Laser ablation at the periphery of podocytes induced CaAR and led to subsequent actin accumulation at the wounding site.
source: Similar to our observations in HeLa cells, laser ablation at the periphery of podocytes induced CaAR and led to subsequent actin accumulation at the wounding site, which was then efficiently sealed without apparent loss of cellular integrity (Figure 6D, Video 10).
evidence: Direct observation in podocytes shown in Figure 6D and Video 10.

claim: Actin accumulation at the wound in podocytes was accompanied by simultaneous induction of lamellipodia in the immediate vicinity.
source: Interestingly, actin accumulation at the wound was accompanied by simultaneous induction of lamellipodia in the immediate vicinity (Figure 6D).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MCF-7 cells that had undergone CaAR upon ATP exposure initiated extended basal protrusions that correlated with the end of CaAR.
source: Similarly, when we extended the period of observation in MCF-7 cells that had undergone CaAR upon ATP exposure, we found that they initiated extended basal protrusions that correlated with the end CaAR.
evidence: Direct observation reported in text.

claim: Protrusions emanating from cell-cell junctions collapsed after only 5–10 min.
source: Protrusions emanating from cell-cell junctions collapsed after only 5–10 min, but those appearing at free cell edges persisted for up to 1 hr (Figure 6E, Video 11).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6E and Video 11.

claim: Protrusions appearing at free cell edges persisted for up to 1 hr.
source: Protrusions emanating from cell-cell junctions collapsed after only 5–10 min, but those appearing at free cell edges persisted for up to 1 hr (Figure 6E, Video 11).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6E and Video 11.

claim: CaAR was efficiently induced in all cells surrounding an ablated cell in a monolayer.
source: CaAR was efficiently induced in all surrounding cells and we again observed short-lived protrusions at cell-cell junctions and longer-lived protrusions at free cell edges (Figure 6F, Video 12).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6F and Video 12.

claim: Some cells formed large lamellipodia which rapidly closed the gap left by the ablated cell.
source: In addition, some cells formed large lamellipodia, which rapidly closed the gap left by the ablated cell (Figure 6F).
evidence: Direct observation shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Untreated MCF-7 cells moved into a gap with an average speed of 3 µm/h after 12 hr.
source: After 12 hr, untreated cells had moved in to the gap with an average speed of 3 µm/h, while cells migrating in the presence of 50 µM ATP (and therefore exhibiting CaAR at the onset of the experiment) covered a much larger area with an average speed of 7 µm/h (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct measurement in wound healing assay shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MCF-7 cells migrating in the presence of 50 µM ATP covered a much larger area with an average speed of 7 µm/h after 12 hr.
source: After 12 hr, untreated cells had moved in to the gap with an average speed of 3 µm/h, while cells migrating in the presence of 50 µM ATP (and therefore exhibiting CaAR at the onset of the experiment) covered a much larger area with an average speed of 7 µm/h (Figure 7B).
evidence: Direct measurement in wound healing assay shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ATP treatment led to an acceleration for the initial 4 hr of migration and cells then reverted to the speed of control cells.
source: A more detailed analysis revealed that ATP treatment led to an acceleration for the initial 4 hr of migration and that cells then reverted to the speed of control cells (Figure 7C, Video 13).
evidence: Direct measurement in wound healing assay shown in Figure 7C and Video 13.

claim: ATP-mediated calcium influx and CaAR are associated with prolonged activation of protrusion and collective migration of MCF-7 cells.
source: Our findings clearly show that ATP-mediated calcium influx and CaAR are associated with prolonged activation of protrusion and collective migration of MCF-7 cells.
evidence: Conclusion from wound healing experiments.

claim: Increased intracellular calcium levels lead to transient and global reorganization of actin in a wide range of epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial and hematopoietic cell lines.
source: We have now found that increased intracellular calcium levels lead to transient and global reorganization of actin in a wide range of epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial and hematopoietic cell lines.
evidence: Summary of observations across multiple cell types.

claim: CaAR is characterized by simultaneous actin polymerization at the ER and disassembly of cortical actin filaments.
source: This reorganization can be triggered by various mechanical and biochemical signals and is characterized by simultaneous actin polymerization at the ER and disassembly of cortical actin filaments.
evidence: Summary of key features of CaAR.

claim: CaAR can act as a morphogenetic integrator during acute cellular perturbations, such as cell cortex damage and wound healing.
source: In agreement with this idea, we found that CaAR can act as a morphogenetic integrator during acute cellular perturbations, such as cell cortex damage and wound healing.
evidence: Conclusion from wound repair and migration experiments.

claim: The highly synchronous kinetics of actin polymerization at the ER and actin disassembly at the cell cortex strongly suggests that competition for a common pool of actin monomers occurs between actin nucleators at the two locations.
source: The highly synchronous kinetics of actin polymerization at the ER and actin disassembly at the cell cortex strongly suggests that competition for a common pool of actin monomers occurs between actin nucleators at the two locations.
evidence: Inference from kinetic observations.

claim: Competition between different actin structures within the same cell has recently been demonstrated for fission yeast cells.
source: Such competition between different actin structures within the same cell has recently been demonstrated for fission yeast cells (Burke et al., 2014; Suarez et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citations.

claim: The stochastic model for CaAR shows that the extent and speed of actin reorganization at the cortex and ER can only be achieved if Ca2+ simultaneously increases the rate of nucleation at the ER and the overall rate of actin depolymerization.
source: Our stochastic model for CaAR shows that the extent and speed of actin reorganization at the cortex and ER can only be achieved if Ca2+ simultaneously increases the rate of nucleation at the ER and the overall rate of actin depolymerization.
evidence: Conclusion from computational modeling.

claim: Ca2+-mediated activation of INF2 could account for all the experimentally observed kinetics of CaAR.
source: Ca2+-mediated activation of INF2 could therefore account for all the experimentally observed kinetics.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling and experimental validation.

claim: SRF/MRTF-dependent transcription is activated by Rho GTPase and mDia-mediated actin dynamics.
source: It is well established that SRF/MRTF-dependent transcription is activated by Rho GTPase and mDia-mediated actin dynamics (Hill et al., 1995; Miralles et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement of established mechanism with citations.

claim: CaAR provides an alternative, INF2-mediated, mechanism for MRTF activation.
source: We have found that CaAR provides an alternative, INF2-mediated, mechanism for MRTF activation.
evidence: Conclusion from MRTF translocation and transcriptome experiments.

claim: There is a strong overlap between CaAR-regulated and classical serum-induced genes.
source: Interestingly, although CaAR is independent of both Rho and serum, we find a strong overlap between CaAR-regulated and classical serum-induced genes.
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: Many of the CaAR-induced genes are associated with cytoskeletal organization, cell adhesion or signaling.
source: Many of the CaAR-induced genes are associated with cytoskeletal organization, cell adhesion or signaling.
evidence: Analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: CaAR is a fundamental process linking Ca2+ signaling, cell mechanics, actin dynamics and SRF-mediated transcription.
source: In summary, we have identified CaAR as a fundamental process linking Ca2+ signaling, cell mechanics, actin dynamics and SRF-mediated transcription.
evidence: Summary conclusion from all experiments.

claim: The strong association of CaAR-induced genes with cancer, inflammation and stress point to opportunities for future studies of CaAR in living organisms.
source: The strong association of CaAR-induced genes with cancer, inflammation and stress point to exciting opportunities for future studies of CaAR in living organisms.
evidence: Speculation based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: INF2 is known to regulate actin dynamics in podocytes.
source: Of particular note is a potential role of CaAR in kidney pathology, as INF2 is known to regulate actin dynamics in podocytes, and INF2 mutations are linked to hereditary kidney diseases (Brown et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citations.

claim: INF2 mutations are linked to hereditary kidney diseases.
source: Of particular note is a potential role of CaAR in kidney pathology, as INF2 is known to regulate actin dynamics in podocytes, and INF2 mutations are linked to hereditary kidney diseases (Brown et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement based on prior literature with citations.
